claim.pdf_says: Items f) and g) are printed indented one level under general rule 9) (begun on page 77); the following items 10), 11), 12), 13) return to the outer level flush with 9).
claim.markdown_says: 'f) When a match occurs between pseudo-text-1 and the library text ...' and 'g) The comparison operation continues ...' begin at column 0, at exactly the same indentation as the immediately following '10) If the REPLACING phrase is specified ...'.
claim.why_it_matters: f) and g) are sub-items of general rule 9) but render as siblings of general rule 10). A reader or a tool citing 7.2.3.4 GR 9 f) cannot tell from the markdown that f) and g) belong to rule 9) rather than being top-level rules of 7.2.3.4.

verdict.reasoning:
The two physical observations in the claim are correct, but the finding is a whitespace/formatting artifact, not a content discrepancy, and its stated consequence is demonstrably false.

WHAT THE PDF ACTUALLY SHOWS (measured, not eyeballed). Column-ink profiling of spec_p79.png at 300 dpi gives, in original pixels: the 'f)' label at left edge x=408 and the 'g)' label at x=408, with their body/hanging-indent text at x=481; the '10)', '11)', '12)', '13)' labels at x=338 with their body text at x=408. The lettered items are therefore indented exactly one hanging-indent step (408-338 = 70 px, ~0.23 in) deeper than the numbered items, and the numbered items' body column (408) coincides with the lettered items' label column - textbook nested-list layout. The claim's description of the PDF is accurate. The markdown slice does put 'f)', 'g)', '10)'..'13)' all at column 0. So the raw observation is not disputed.

WHY IT IS NOT A REAL FINDING.

1) No content differs. Every word of f), g), 10), 11), 12) and 13) is present in specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 3507-3517, verbatim, in the correct order, with no omission, insertion, reflow error or misquotation. Nothing is 'misplaced' - the claimed kind is wrong. The sole difference is leading whitespace.

2) The nesting level is still unambiguously encoded, by the label glyphs themselves. 7.2.3.4 General rules is a NUMERIC list: 1) through 13) (markdown lines 3451-3517). There is no lettered top-level list anywhere in 7.2.3.4. An item labelled 'f)' or 'g)' therefore cannot be read as a top-level rule of 7.2.3.4 - the alphabet of the label is itself the level marker. The claim's 'why it matters' asserts precisely the confusion that the label scheme makes impossible.

3) Ownership is recoverable from the immediate text, and the markdown is read as a continuous document, not as an isolated page. Line 3467 reads '9) The comparison operation to determine text replacement occurs in the following manner:' - a colon lead-in - and is immediately followed by a) at line 3469, then b)-e) on page 78 and f)-g) here. The parent of the a)..g) run is stated in words by rule 9) itself.

4) It is not a page-79 defect at all; it is a document-wide transcription convention. The same flattening applies to b), c), d) and e) on page 78 (markdown lines 3476, 3478, 3498, 3500), all at column 0, and to the sub-sub items 1.-6. under c) (lines 3480-3494). Only the very first item a) (line 3469) retained a 3-space indent. Ledgering this as a structural finding against page 79 would mis-scope a global whitespace-normalization property of the OCR/markdown pipeline as a localized content error, and the identical finding could be filed against essentially every nested list in the document.

5) Page-break furniture is in fact handled CORRECTLY here, which cuts against the claim. The paragraph printed at the top of PDF page 79 ('is then considered as the leftmost library text-word, and the comparison cycle starts again with the first pseudo-text-1 or partial-word-1 specified in the REPLACING phrase.') is the wrapped tail of item e); the markdown correctly joins it to e) at the end of line 3500 rather than stranding it. So the transcription preserved the one genuine cross-page content relationship on this page.

Meaning is unchanged and fully recoverable; the difference is indentation only. Per the standing rule that formatting-only differences that do not change meaning are rejected, this is not a real discrepancy.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. Confirmed physically: in the PDF the f)/g) labels sit at x=408 and the 10)-13) labels at x=338 (300 dpi), one hanging-indent step apart, while the markdown places all of them at column 0. But no text is missing, altered or reordered - only leading whitespace is lost. The level remains encoded by the labels themselves (7.2.3.4's top-level rules are numeric 1)-13); there is no lettered top-level list), and rule 9)'s colon lead-in names the parent in words, so f) and g) cannot be mistaken for top-level rules as the claim asserts. The flattening is a document-wide convention of the transcription (b)-e) on page 78 and the 1.-6. sub-list under c) are equally flush left; only a) on page 77 kept a 3-space indent), not a page-79 fault. If this is to be tracked at all, it belongs as a single global 'nested-list indentation is not preserved' note about the conversion pipeline, at cosmetic severity - not as a per-page structural misplaced-content finding.
